Unveiling nonmagnetic phase and many-body entanglement in
two-dimensional random quantum magnets Sr2CuTe1-xWxO6

Dian Wu Email: dian.wu@epfl.ch Affiliation: Institute of Physics, École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), CH-1015 Lausanne, Switzerland    Fan Yang Email: f.yang@epfl.ch Affiliation: Institute of Physics, École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), CH-1015 Lausanne, Switzerland    Giuseppe Carleo Email: giuseppe.carleo@epfl.ch Affiliation: Institute of Physics, École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), CH-1015 Lausanne, Switzerland
August 24, 2026
Abstract

We apply a random-plaquette J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} model on the square lattice to capture the physics of a series of spin-1/21/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnet compounds Sr2CuTe1-xWxO6. With the input of experimentally relevant coupling strengths, our exact diagonalization (ED) study probes the ground state properties beyond previous linear spin-wave approach. An intermediate range of x∈[0.08,0.55]x\in[0.08,0.55] is identified for a nonmagnetic phase without the long-range Néel or stripe order. The absence of both valence-bond-glass order and spin-glass non-ergodic dynamics renders its nature intriguing. Deep inside this phase around x=0.3x=0.3, we observe signatures potentially linked to randomness-induced short-range spin-liquid-like (SLL) states, including close to zero spin-freezing parameter, vanishing spin-spin correlation beyond nearest neighbors, almost uniform static spin structure factor, as well as a broad tail in the dynamical spin structure factor. The nonmagnetic phase also features multipartite entanglement in the ground state witnessed by quantum Fisher information (QFI), which exhibits universal scaling behaviors at quantum critical points.

I Introduction

Quantum spin liquids (QSLs) [1, 2, 3], as ground states of disordered quantum spins characteristic of vanishing long-range magnetic order and massive many-body entanglement, have renewed theoretical and experimental interests [4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9] in recent years. From a few exactly solvable examples, such as the Kitaev ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} spin liquids in the spin-1/21/2 honeycomb model [10] with generalizations to ladder geometries [11, 12], the triangle-honeycomb [13] and three-dimensional lattices [14], as well as extensions to higher-spin analogues [15], it is well known that certain types of QSL feature fractional excitations of quasiparticles, including anyons [16] and Majorana zero modes [17, 18], which can be adapted into braiding and fusion mechanisms [10, 19] leading to potential fault-tolerant quantum computation [20, 21].

Pursuing QSLs in experimental platforms proves to be challenging. Quantum simulators [22, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27] offer precise control of spin exchange interactions, yet remain to be scaled up to large system sizes. Quantum materials of frustrated magnets [28, 4, 29, 8, 9, 30], on the other hand, deviate from the ideal frustration scenarios set up in simple models, and more often than not involve intrinsic inhomogeneity or quenched randomness, which results in disorder on sites or bonds. Meanwhile, motivated by theoretical concerns on finding more methods to directly observe many-body entanglement as independent evidence for quantum critical phenomena in strongly correlated systems [31, 32, 33, 34], there arise increasing interests and efforts in probing entanglement properties in quantum materials [35, 36, 37, 38, 39, 40], and establishing links with quantum information science [41, 42].

In this work, we focus on the spin-1/21/2 square-lattice Heisenberg antiferromagnet: the double perovskite Sr2CuTe1-xWxO6 [44, 45, 46, 47, 48, 49, 50, 43, 51, 52], whose degrees of frustration and randomness can be tuned by the mixing ratio xx of Te and W ions. At x=0x=0 and 11, the compounds Sr2CuTeO6 and Sr2CuWO6 are illustrated by the first two panels of Fig. 1 (a). They are dominated by nearest-neighbor J1J_{1} and next-nearest-neighbor J2J_{2} Heisenberg antiferromagnetic (AFM) interactions and also have weak frustrated interactions J2′J^{\prime}_{2} and J1′J^{\prime}_{1}, thus exhibit the Néel order and the stripe order respectively, as in Fig. 1 (b). While nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) experiments [44, 45] suggest a SLL state in between, numerical attempts to reveal its nature become challenging both in the choice of effective spin models, and in the absence of lattice symmetry and translational symmetry due to disorder. Preliminary ED computations on the random-bond J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} model point to a random-singlet phase and a spin-glass phase [53], while density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) studies find evidence only of the random-singlet state [54]. The latter is in agreement with quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) simulations on the random JJ-QQ model [55] with JJ the Heisenberg exchange and QQ the multispin interaction. The two effective models studied so far are remotely linked to the material and the role of the mixing ratio xx remains obscure.

Here, we focus on a different and more realistic microscopic description [43], the random-plaquette J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} model depicted in Fig. 1 (a). In the two-dimensional square lattice, each plaquette can be J2J_{2}-dominated (W counterion) with probability xx, and otherwise J1J_{1}-dominated (Te counterion). When two different kinds of plaquette are adjacent, i.e., when a Te and a W counterions encounter, the strong J1J_{1} bond on the shared edge is replaced by a weaker J1′′J^{\prime\prime}_{1} bond. From the linear spin-wave approach [43, 52], the random-plaquette model is found to faithfully reproduce the inelastic neutron scattering spectra, the magnetic excitations, as well as the neutron diffraction patterns of Sr2CuTe1-xWxO6. Moreover, Monte Carlo simulations show that even with classical spins, this model can explain the extreme suppression of the Néel order at small x=0.025x=0.025, consistent with muon spin resonance (μ\muSR) measurements [51]. Yet, a computational simulation of the quantum model is still lacking.

Throughout this work, we present a comprehensive ED study of the model with quantum spins. We take Heisenberg AFM coupling strengths obtained from quantum chemistry calculations [43]:

(J1,J2,J1′,J2′,J1′′)=(7.4, 8.3, 0.7, 0.1, 0.3),(J_{1},\ J_{2},\ J^{\prime}_{1},\ J^{\prime}_{2},\ J^{\prime\prime}_{1})=(7.4,\ 8.3,\ 0.7,\ 0.1,\ 0.3), (1)

in the unit of meV. Remarkably, as shown in Fig. 1 (b) and Fig. 2 (a)–(d), from the order parameters we identify a nonmagnetic ground state for Sr2CuTe1-xWxO6 in a wide range of x∈[0.08,0.55]x\in[0.08,0.55], matching well with the NMR observations [44, 45, 46] that there is no magnetic order over 1919 mK for x∈[0.1,0.6]x\in[0.1,0.6]. On top of this, the universal scaling exponent of the QFI density [32, 36, 37] extracted from the static spin structure factor vanishes near the phase boundaries, confirming the accuracy of our phase diagram.

The nature of the intermediate phase is distinct from normal candidates previously found in quantum magnets subject to quenched randomness, including the random-singlet state [53, 54, 55, 56, 57, 58], the valence-bond glass [46, 59, 60], and the spin glass [53, 36, 37]. Instead, its main features are more akin to short-range disordered SLL states in two dimensions, which have an extremely small spin-freezing parameter and a broad tail in the dynamical spin structure factor. Intriguingly, deep inside the nonmagnetic phase around x=0.3x=0.3 where these characteristics become the most predominant, the system displays zero averaged spin-spin correlation beyond nearest neighbors, and almost uniformly distributed static spin structure factor, leading to a uniform QFI density at T=0T=0.

The paper is structured as follows. In Section II, based on ED computations, we perform finite-size scaling of the order parameters and determine the phase diagram for the random-plaquette J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} model. We characterize the emergent short-range disordered SLL state by spin-spin correlations, spin relaxations, as well as spin structure factors. In Section III, we focus on the QFI and reveal its universal scaling behaviors at quantum phase transitions. In Section IV, we advance the understanding of the phase formation in Sr2CuTe1-xWxO6 qualitatively through the randomness-induced frustration index.

II Properties of the model

Before proceeding to study physical observables, we first briefly introduce our reweighting method to compute the observables, which enables us to obtain the disorder-averaged ground-state expectation values with an arbitrary mixing ratio x∈[0,1]x\in[0,1]. For each system size N=8,12,16,20,24,28,32N=8,12,16,20,24,28,32, we construct a lattice whose geometry allows both Néel and stripe orders under periodic boundary conditions (PBC). Then for each k=0,1,…,Nk=0,1,\ldots,N, we randomly generate MkM_{k} Hamiltonian instances, each with exactly kk J2J_{2}-dominated plaquettes. As xx is the probability for a plaquette to be J2J_{2}-dominated in the disorder average, any physical observable OO is averaged under a binomial distribution, denoted by [⋯]J[\,\cdots]_{J}:

[⟨O⟩]J​(N,x)=∑kB⁡(k,N,x)​O¯k​(N),\displaystyle\left[\!\expectationvalue*{O}\right]_{J}(N,x)=\sum_{k}B(k,N,x)\bar{O}_{k}(N), (2)
O¯k​(N)=1Mk​∑i⟨O⟩i,\displaystyle\bar{O}_{k}(N)=\frac{1}{M_{k}}\sum_{i}\expectationvalue*{O}_{i}, (3)

where the binomial distribution takes the form B⁡(k,N,x)=(Nk)​xk​(1−x)N−kB(k,N,x)=\binom{N}{k}x^{k}(1-x)^{N-k}, and the binomial coefficient reads (Nk)=N!/(k!​(N−k)!)\binom{N}{k}=N!/(k!\,(N-k)!). In O¯k​(N)\bar{O}_{k}(N), the expectation ⟨O⟩i\expectationvalue*{O}_{i} acts on the ground state of the random instance ii. Without reweighting, O¯k​(N)\bar{O}_{k}(N) alone is an estimator of the uniform average over all random instances with a fixed kk, under which circumstance xx can only take discrete values k/Nk/N with a finite system size NN. Our reweighting method makes it possible to vary xx continuously and more precisely determine the phase boundaries, as shown in the right column of Fig. 2. More details on the ED computation, including choices of lattice geometries, reweighting, and estimation of uncertainties in the average and the extrapolation, can be found in Appendix A.

We comment on the symmetries of the ground state. It inherits the SU(2)(2) symmetry from Heisenberg exchanges, leading to zero magnetization ⟨Sjz⟩=0\expectationvalue*{S^z_j}=0 for each site jj. The ground state also respects spin inversion symmetry and selects the even parity sector for all lattices we use, regardless of the value of xx and the configuration of random plaquettes. Translational symmetry and D4D_{4} lattice symmetry, by contrast, are only present at x=0x=0 and 11.

II.1 Order parameters and phase diagram

Now, we determine the phase diagram of the random-plaquette J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} model (see Fig. 1) from four order parameters shown in Fig. 2. While the Néel and the stripe order parameters set the boundaries of two magnetically ordered phases when xx is close to 00 and 11 respectively, the spin-freezing parameter and the valence-bond-glass parameter suggest that the nonmagnetic region x∈[0.08,0.55]x\in[0.08,0.55] cannot stabilize a random-singlet state nor a valence-bond glass.

First, let us take a closer look at two magnetically ordered phases. We choose the following definitions [53] for the Néel and the stripe order parameters:

mN2\displaystyle m_{\text{N}}^{2} =8N⁡(N+4)​[∑α∑i,j∈α⟨𝑺i⋅𝑺j⟩]J,\displaystyle=\frac{8}{N(N+4)}\left[\sum_{\alpha}\sum_{i,j\in\alpha}\!\expectationvalue*{\bm{S}_i \cdot\bm{S}_j}\right]_{J}, (4)
mstr2\displaystyle m_{\text{str}}^{2} =4N⁡(N+4)​[∑ν∑αν∑i,j∈αν⟨𝑺i⋅𝑺j⟩]J.\displaystyle=\frac{4}{N(N+4)}\left[\sum_{\nu}\,\sum_{\alpha_{\nu}}\sum_{i,j\in\alpha_{\nu}}\!\!\expectationvalue*{\bm{S}_i \cdot\bm{S}_j}\right]_{J}. (5)

In mN2m_{\text{N}}^{2}, α\alpha denotes each of the two sublattices formed by the Néel order, as shown in different colors in Fig. 1 (b), and i,ji,j run over all sites in the sublattice α\alpha. In mstr2m_{\text{str}}^{2}, ν\nu denotes each of the two directions of stripes, giving rise to two patterns of sublattices αν\alpha_{\nu}. Figure 1 (b) depicts the horizontal stripes, and vertical otherwise. The disorder average [⋯]J[\,\cdots]_{J} is evaluated using our reweighting method in Eq. 2. The normalization factors in Eqs. 4 and 5 are chosen according to relevant magnetic orderings of the classical Heisenberg antiferromagnet. For a perfect Néel order, the sum inside [⋯]J[\,\cdots]_{J} in mN2m_{\text{N}}^{2} containing both i=ji=j and i≠ji\neq j amounts to 2​(N2⋅34+N2​(N2−1)⋅14)=N⁡(N+4)/82\left(\frac{N}{2}\cdot\frac{3}{4}+\frac{N}{2}(\frac{N}{2}-1)\cdot\frac{1}{4}\right)=N(N+4)/8. The factor in mstr2m_{\text{str}}^{2} is further multiplied by 22 taking into account two types of stripes ν\nu. We then perform a finite-size scaling with 8≤N≤328\leq N\leq 32, as shown in Fig. 2 (a)–(d). It turns out that both order parameters exhibit N−1/2N^{-1/2} scaling behaviors, consistent with the modified spin-wave analysis for Heisenberg antiferromagnet on finite square lattices [61, 62]:

⟨𝑺i⋅𝑺j⟩=(−1)α⁡(i,j)​(c0+c1|𝒓i−𝒓j|)2,i≠j,\expectationvalue*{\bm{S}_i \cdot\bm{S}_j}=(-1)^{\alpha(i,j)}\left(c_{0}+\frac{c_{1}}{|\bm{r}_{i}-\bm{r}_{j}|}\right)^{2},\quad i\neq j, (6)

where both c0c_{0} and c1c_{1} are constant given a finite NN. The sign (−1)α⁡(i,j)=1(-1)^{\alpha(i,j)}=1 if the sites ii and jj belong to the same sublattice α\alpha, and −1-1 otherwise. Equation 6 leads directly to the scaling relation:

mN/str2=aN+b,b≥0,m_{\text{N/str}}^{2}=\frac{a}{\sqrt{N}}+b,\quad b\geq 0, (7)

where higher order corrections in O⁡(1/N)O(1/N) are neglected. In the thermodynamic limit N→∞N\to\infty, if the long-range magnetic order exists, mN2m_{\text{N}}^{2} and mstr2m_{\text{str}}^{2} become positive constants. From the non-negative extrapolation values of mN2m_{\text{N}}^{2} and mstr2m_{\text{str}}^{2} in Fig. 2 (b) and (d), we identify that in the ground state, the Néel phase survives from the randomness when x∈[0,0.08]x\in[0,0.08] and the stripe phase survives when x∈[0.55,1]x\in[0.55,1]. The two quantum phase transition points crossing zero are resolved as xc,1=0.081±0.012x_{c,1}=0.081\pm 0.012, xc,2=0.546±0.020x_{c,2}=0.546\pm 0.020. The extremely narrow region of the Néel order compared with the stripe order can be explained by reviewing the microscopic structure of the mixed compound in Fig. 1 (a). When two different kinds of plaquette encounter, one strong J1J_{1} bond is replaced by a much weaker J1′′J^{\prime\prime}_{1} bond on the shared edge, while the strong J2J_{2} bonds in the J2J_{2}-dominated plaquette remain unaffected.

The consistency of our nonmagnetic phase in absence of long-range order for x∈[0.08,0.55]x\in[0.08,0.55] with the experimental results x∈[0.1,0.6]x\in[0.1,0.6] [44, 45, 46] is crucial. It validates the methodology of the current work, including the Hamiltonian we start with in Eq. 1, our ED computations, as well as our reweighting method in Eq. 2 and extrapolation method. Next, we proceed to explore the nature of the nonmagnetic phase by testing two potential candidates: the random-singlet state and the valence-bond glass.

The random-singlet state can be characterized by the the spin-freezing parameter [53, 54], also known as the Edwards–Anderson (EA) order parameter [63, 64], defined by

qEA2=1N2​[∑i,j⟨𝑺i⋅𝑺j⟩2]J,q_{\text{EA}}^{2}=\frac{1}{N^{2}}\left[\sum_{i,j}\expectationvalue*{\bm{S}_i \cdot\bm{S}_j}^{2}\right]_{J}, (8)

where ∑i\sum_{i} sums over a total number of NN sites. qEAq_{\text{EA}} detects any type of static spin order, including long-range magnetic orders and the spin-glass order. In Fig. 2 (e)–(f), qEAq_{\text{EA}} scales with N−1/2N^{-1/2} and extrapolates to positive values as N→∞N\to\infty for all xx, with the nonmagentic region x∈[0.08,0.55]x\in[0.08,0.55] locating a plateau around its minimum. The inset in (f) shows that the error bars of the extrapolation in the nonmagnetic phase do not extend to zero, and the average value of the plateau stays at 0.017±0.0040.017\pm 0.004. Our finding agrees with the linear spin-wave analysis [52] of the same model in Eq. 1 that the degree of frustration arising from weak Heisenberg interactions J1′,J2′,J1′′J^{\prime}_{1},J^{\prime}_{2},J^{\prime\prime}_{1} is not strong enough to stabilize an all-to-all disordered random-singlet state in Sr2CuTe1-xWxO6.

The valence-bond glass (VBG), on the other hand, can be characterized by an order parameter that replaces the spin operator in qEAq_{\text{EA}} with the dimer operator [65]:

qVBG2=14​N2​[∑i,j∑p,q⟨Bip​Bjq⟩2]J,\displaystyle q_{\text{VBG}}^{2}=\frac{1}{4N^{2}}\left[\sum_{i,j}\sum_{p,q}\expectationvalue*{B_i^p B_j^q}^{2}\right]_{J}, (9)
Bip=𝑺i⋅𝑺i+p−⟨𝑺i⋅𝑺i+p⟩,\displaystyle B_{i}^{p}=\bm{S}_{i}\cdot\bm{S}_{i+p}-\expectationvalue*{\bm{S}_i \cdot\bm{S}_{i + p}}, (10)

where BipB_{i}^{p} encodes the dimer-dimer correlation [66] on a nearest-neighbor bond along the unit vector pp, and pp can be either in xx or yy direction, i.e., ∑i∑p\sum_{i}\sum_{p} sums over a total number of 2​N2N nearest-neighbor bonds. As shown in Fig. 2 (g)–(h), qVBGq_{\text{VBG}} also exhibits N−1/2N^{-1/2} scaling behavior, but extrapolates to negative values as N→∞N\to\infty for all xx. We have also tested another dimer operator that sums over both nearest and next-nearest bonds and obtained the same behavior. Therefore, the putative valence-bond-glass state from the specific heat measurement at low temperatures [46], is not observed by our ED results of the random-plaquette model at T=0T=0.

II.2 Short-range spin-spin correlations and non-glassy dynamics in the nonmagnetic phase

A small but finite qEAq_{\text{EA}} when N→∞N\to\infty could indicate a weak spin-glass order. However, as we will show in this section through spin-spin correlations over space and time domains, see Figs. 3 and 4, the spin glass is also not a candidate for the nonmagnetic phase.

First, let us examine the spin-spin correlation in real space,

Cr=[⟨𝑺i⋅𝑺j⟩]J,𝒓,r=|𝒓i−𝒓j|.C_{r}=\left[\expectationvalue*{\bm{S}_i \cdot\bm{S}_j}\right]_{J,\bm{r}},\quad r=|\bm{r}_{i}-\bm{r}_{j}|. (11)

Besides the disorder average [⋯]J[\,\cdots]_{J} over all random instances in Eq. 2, we also take the average over all spin pairs (i,j)(i,j) sharing the same distance rr in each random instance [67]. Figure 3 shows that while the Néel (stripe) order is indicated by the dominant negative correlations at nearest-neighbor r=1r=1 (next-nearest-neighbor r=2r=\sqrt{2}), the long-range spin-spin correlations decrease quickly when xx enters the nonmagnetic phase. In particular, deep inside this phase around x=0.3x=0.3, we observe zero spin-spin correlation beyond nearest neighbors. The remaining AFM spin-spin correlations on nearest neighbors contribute to the non-zero extrapolation of spin-freezing parameter qEAq_{\text{EA}} in Fig. 2 (e)–(f), and it is incompatible with the random domain wall picture of the spin-glass state in the random-bond J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} model. According to Ref. [53], the latter would host a considerable amount of positive ferromagnetic (FM) correlations on nearest-neighbor spins across the domain walls between two distinct stripe-ordered states. In our model, the randomness-induced frustration plays a more important role, of which we leave the discussion to Section IV.

Next, we study the temporal auto-correlation of one spin in the ground state, which can probe the ergodicity breaking in finite-size glassy systems [68]:

Ct=[⟨{Sz†(t),Sz(0)}⟩]J,C_{t}=\left[\expectationvalue*{\{S^{z \dagger}(t), S^z(0)\}}\right]_{J}, (12)

where Sz†(t)=ei​H​tSz(0)e−i​H​tS^{z\dagger}(t)=e^{iHt}S^{z}(0)e^{-iHt}, and Ct∈ℝC_{t}\in\mathbb{R} since Sz†(t)=Sz(t)S^{z\dagger}(t)=S^{z}(t). It is noted that the choice of the spin SzS^{z} in the system is arbitrary after averaging over random instances, and the zz orientation is also arbitrary as the model is SU​(2)\text{SU}(2) symmetric. In Fig. 4, the two magnetically ordered phases at x=0x=0 and 11 exhibit oscillating patterns that do not decay at large tt. By contrast, in the nonmagnetic phase x∈[0.08,0.55]x\in[0.08,0.55], the auto-correlation relaxes to zero quickly. We do not observe the non-ergodic behavior in CtC_{t} that is characteristic of a spin glass, which would entail a long-lived plateau at large tt.

II.3 Static and dynamical spin structure factors

After invalidating three candidates, namely random-singlet state, valence-bond glass, and spin glass, we proceed to unveil nontrivial SLL signatures of the nonmagnetic phase through spin structure factors.

The static spin structure factor defined by

Ssta​(𝒌)=1N​[∑i,j⟨𝑺i⋅𝑺j⟩​cos⁡(𝒌⋅(𝒓i−𝒓j))]J,S_{\text{sta}}(\bm{k})=\frac{1}{N}\left[\sum_{i,j}\expectationvalue*{\bm{S}_i \cdot\bm{S}_j}\cos\left(\bm{k}\cdot(\bm{r}_{i}-\bm{r}_{j})\right)\right]_{J}, (13)

is resolved in the ground state via ED in Fig. 5, in close resemblance to the experimental data probed by diffuse polarized neutron diffraction at T=1.5T=1.5 K [52]. As xx increases from 00 (Néel order) to 11 (stripe order), the peak of SstaS_{\text{sta}} moves from (π,π)(\pi,\pi) to (π,0)(\pi,0). Meanwhile, Fig. 5 shows a more detailed feature that the peak becomes less sharp once xx leaves the ordered phases and approaches the phase boundaries at x=0.1x=0.1 and 0.50.5, which also agrees with the experimental data. Interestingly, around x=0.3x=0.3, SstaS_{\text{sta}} becomes almost uniform in a large portion of the Brillouin zone (BZ) without any visible peak. It indicates a strongly disordered state, absent of any long-range magnetic order.

Furthermore, as shown from the dynamical spin structure factor in Fig. 6, the coexistence of a peak centered at a small frequency ω\omega and a broad tail at large ω\omega also supports a SLL state [53, 65] in the nonmagnetic region around x=0.3x=0.3. In our calculation, we adopt the following definition for the dynamical spin structure factor:

Sdyn​(𝒌,ω)\displaystyle S_{\text{dyn}}(\bm{k},\omega) =12​π​∫−∞∞[⟨Sz†𝒌(t)Sz𝒌(0)⟩]J​ei​ω​t​dt\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\left[\expectationvalue*{S^{z \dagger}_{\bm{k}}(t) S^z_{\bm{k}}(0)}\right]_{J}\!e^{i\omega t}\differential t (14)
=−limη→0[1πIm⟨Sz†𝒌1ω+E0−H+i​ηSz𝒌⟩]J,\displaystyle=-\lim_{\eta\to 0}\left[\frac{1}{\pi}\imaginary\expectationvalue*{S^{z \dagger}_{\bm{k}} \frac{1}{\omega+ E_0 - H + i \eta} S^z_{\bm{k}}}\right]_{J},

with E0E_{0} the ground state energy. The time-domain integral is computed using continued fraction expansion [69] and smoothed with a sufficiently small damping factor η=0.1\eta=0.1 meV [53, 65]. The Fourier transform of a spin operator is taken to be

Sz𝒌=1N∑i=1NSize−i𝒌⋅𝒓i.S^{z}_{\bm{k}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{i=1}^{N}S_{i}^{z}e^{-i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{r}_{i}}. (15)

Figure 6 shows that when the mixing ratio xx increases in the nonmagnetic region, the peak of SdynS_{\text{dyn}} moves in the BZ from the center (π,π)(\pi,\pi) to the edge (π,0)(\pi,0). In the frequency domain, the peak moves towards smaller ω\omega as the randomness xx increases at 𝒌=(π,π)\bm{k}=(\pi,\pi), while at (π,0)(\pi,0) it stays rather fixed near ω≈2\omega\approx 2 meV. Most importantly, taking into account the flatness of the static spin structure factor in the nonmagnetic phase in Fig. 5, the broad peak of SdynS_{\text{dyn}} extends naturally to other wave vectors in the BZ. This behavior can be used to distinguish from magnon-like excitations which introduce peaks only at high-symmetry points of the BZ [65]. We have also tested finite-size effects and verified that for a fixed x∈[0.08,0.55]x\in[0.08,0.55] at both wave vectors, the peak reaches lower frequency as the system size increases.

III Quantum Fisher information in 2D random quantum magnets

In this section, we introduce the general relation between the QFI and the spin structure factors, and demonstrate how to use the QFI density as a witness of multipartite entanglement in the random-plaquette J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} model.

III.1 Multipartite entanglement witness

Let us start from a generic equilibrium mixed state at the temperature TT. Its density matrix has the form ρ=∑λpλ​|λ⟩​⟨λ|\rho=\sum_{\lambda}p_{\lambda}\ket{\lambda}\bra{\lambda} with the probability pλ=1Ze−Eλ/Tp_{\lambda}=\frac{1}{Z}e^{-E_{\lambda}/T} and the partition function Z=∑λe−Eλ/TZ=\sum_{\lambda}e^{-E_{\lambda}/T}, where we set ℏ=kB=1\hbar=k_{B}=1. Given a generator O=∑i=1NOiO=\sum_{i=1}^{N}O_{i} consisting of local operators OiO_{i} that are normalized with unit spectrum width, the QFI is defined by

fQ​(T)=2​∑λ,λ′(pλ−pλ′)2pλ+pλ′​|⟨λ|O|λ′⟩|2,f_{\text{Q}}(T)=2\sum_{\lambda,\lambda^{\prime}}\frac{(p_{\lambda}-p_{\lambda^{\prime}})^{2}}{p_{\lambda}+p_{\lambda^{\prime}}}\left|\!\matrixelement{\lambda}{O}{\lambda'}\right|^{2}, (16)

with pλ+pλ′>0p_{\lambda}+p_{\lambda^{\prime}}>0. Physically, through the quantum Cramér–Rao bound [70], fQf_{\text{Q}} quantifies the maximal precision of a parameter θ\theta one can reach after MM independent measurements: Var⁡θ≥1/(M​fQ)\Var\theta\geq 1/(Mf_{\text{Q}}). It is a lower bound for the variance of parameter θ\theta associated with the generator OO. Under each measurement, the system undergoes a unitary transformation: ρ′=e−i​θ​O​ρ​ei​θ​O\rho^{\prime}=e^{-i\theta O}\rho e^{i\theta O}. The QFI has been successfully measured in a single spin system, or a solid-state qubit [71].

Going to multispin systems of higher complexity, an exact relation can be established [32, 36, 37] between the QFI density fQ=fQ/Nf_{\text{Q}}=f_{\text{Q}}/N and the dynamical spin structure factor SdynS_{\text{dyn}}:

fQ​(𝒌,T)=4​∫0∞tanh⁡(ω2​T)⁡(1−e−ωT)​Sdyn​(𝒌,ω,T)​dω,f_{\text{Q}}(\bm{k},T)=4\int_{0}^{\infty}\!\!\tanh(\frac{\omega}{2 T})\left(1-e^{-\frac{\omega}{T}}\right)S_{\text{dyn}}(\bm{k},\omega,T)\,\differential\omega, (17)

with the generator chosen to be O(𝒌)=NS𝒌z†=∑i=1NSizei​𝒌⋅𝒓iO(\bm{k})=\sqrt{N}S^{z\dagger}_{\bm{k}}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}S_{i}^{z}e^{i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{r}_{i}}. Here, SdynS_{\text{dyn}} is obtained from Eq. 14 by applying ⟨Sz†𝒌(t)Sz𝒌(0)⟩=Tr[ρS𝒌z†(t)S𝒌z(0)]\expectationvalue*{S^{z \dagger}_{\bm{k}}(t) S^z_{\bm{k}}(0)}=\Tr[\rho\,S^{z\dagger}_{\bm{k}}(t)S^{z}_{\bm{k}}(0)], which acts on the thermal state when T>0T>0 and on the ground state at T=0T=0. Equation 17 expresses the entanglement in an explicit form of quantum fluctuations. A detailed derivation is provided in Appendix B.

Notably, a quantum state is (m+1)(m+1)-partite entangled when the QFI density satisfies the inequality [32, 37, 72, 73]: fQ>m​(hmax−hmin)2f_{\text{Q}}>m(h_{\text{max}}-h_{\text{min}})^{2}, where mm is an integer and hmaxh_{\text{max}} (hminh_{\text{min}}) is the largest (smallest) eigenvalue of the local generator OiO_{i}. In our case, ⟨Oi†​Oi⟩=⟨(Siz)2⟩=1/4\expectationvalue*{O^\dagger_i O_i}=\expectationvalue*{(S_i^z)^2}=1/4 and hmax=−hmin=1/2h_{\text{max}}=-h_{\text{min}}=1/2. Therefore, (m+1)(m+1)-partite entanglement is witnessed in a multispin system if

fQ>m.f_{\text{Q}}>m. (18)

At the same time, Eq. 18 sets the criterion according to which the quantum Cramér–Rao bound falls below the classical limits [74].

Next, we focus on the features of the QFI in the ground state of the random-plaquette model. By taking the limit T→0T\to 0 in Eq. 17, we can verify that

fQ​(𝒌)=4​∫0∞Sdyn​(𝒌,ω)​dω=43​Ssta​(𝒌).f_{\text{Q}}(\bm{k})=4\int_{0}^{\infty}S_{\text{dyn}}(\bm{k},\omega)\,\differential\omega=\frac{4}{3}S_{\text{sta}}(\bm{k}). (19)

The extra factor 1/31/3 comes from one of the three SU​(2)\text{SU}(2)-symmetric components 𝑺i⋅𝑺j=∑α=x,y,zSiα​Sjα\bm{S}_{i}\cdot\bm{S}_{j}=\sum_{\alpha=x,y,z}S_{i}^{\alpha}S_{j}^{\alpha}. Equivalently, we can also evaluate the QFI of a pure ground state |ψ⟩\ket{\psi}. The density matrix becomes ρ=|ψ⟩​⟨ψ|\rho=\ket{\psi}\bra{\psi}, and the case pψ=1p_{\psi}=1, pψ′=0p_{\psi^{\prime}}=0 contributes twice to fQf_{\text{Q}} in Eq. 16. Applying the identity |ψ′⟩​⟨ψ′|=𝟙−|ψ⟩​⟨ψ|\ket{\psi'}\bra{\psi'}=\mathds{1}-\ket{\psi}\bra{\psi}, we obtain the same relation

fQ​(𝒌)=4​[⟨Sz𝒌Sz†𝒌⟩−|⟨S𝒌z⟩|2]J=43​Ssta​(𝒌).f_{\text{Q}}(\bm{k})=4\left[\expectationvalue*{S^z_{\bm{k}} S^{z \dagger}_{\bm{k}}}-|\expectationvalue*{S^z_{\bm{k}}}|^{2}\right]_{J}=\frac{4}{3}S_{\text{sta}}(\bm{k}). (20)

It is noted that ⟨S𝒌z⟩=0\expectationvalue*{S^z_{\bm{k}}}=0 respecting the SU​(2)\text{SU}(2) symmetry.

In Fig. 7, we quantify multipartite entanglement witnessed by fQf_{\text{Q}} at the two ordering wave vectors using Eqs. 18 and 19. The nonmagnetic phase is short-range entangled, featuring 22- to 44-partite entanglement on a finite-size lattice of N=32N=32 spins. By contrast, the Néel and the stripe phases possess much higher entanglement at their respective ordering wave vectors. This long-range entanglement is also reflected in the sharp peaks of Ssta​(𝒌)S_{\text{sta}}(\bm{k}) in Fig. 5. When the mixing ratio xx increases from 00 to 11, the peak of fQf_{\text{Q}} moves from 𝒌=(π,π)\bm{k}=(\pi,\pi) to (π,0)(\pi,0) following the same result as SstaS_{\text{sta}}. Around x=0.3x=0.3 deep inside the nonmagnetic phase, fQf_{\text{Q}} also becomes uniform and the system displays bipartite entanglement over the BZ.

III.2 Universal scaling at quantum critical points

Another interesting feature observed from Fig. 7 is that in the finite-size system with N=32N=32, if we choose an ordering wave vector and tunes xx towards the other ordered phase, there is always no multipartite entanglement to be witnessed at the phase boundary, as fQ<1f_{\text{Q}}<1 at 𝒌=(π,π)\bm{k}=(\pi,\pi), x=0.55x=0.55 and 𝒌=(π,0)\bm{k}=(\pi,0), x=0.08x=0.08. In the following, we will demonstrate through the scaling analysis of fQf_{\text{Q}} that in the thermodynamic limit, the critical points for fQ=1f_{\text{Q}}=1 before entering a separable (unentangled) region coincide with the phase boundaries of the random-plaquette model determined by the order parameters.

At T=0T=0, we start from a general scaling relation between the QFI density and the system size:

ln⁡fQ​(𝒌)=νQ​(𝒌)​ln⁡N+c0,\ln f_{\text{Q}}(\bm{k})=\nu_{\text{Q}}(\bm{k})\ln N+c_{0}, (21)

where νQ\nu_{\text{Q}} denotes the scaling exponent and c0c_{0} is a constant. If νQ=0\nu_{\text{Q}}=0, then fQf_{\text{Q}} converges to a finite value when we take the thermodynamic limit N→∞N\to\infty. The finite-size ED computations on our model lead to Fig. 8. At 𝒌=(π,π)\bm{k}=(\pi,\pi), νQ\nu_{\text{Q}} is positive when x<0.55x<0.55 and vanishes as νQ=0.02±0.05\nu_{\text{Q}}=0.02\pm 0.05 around the critical point xc=0.55x_{\text{c}}=0.55. Thus when N→∞N\to\infty, fQf_{\text{Q}} converges to a finite value fQ≈1f_{\text{Q}}\approx 1 only when xx is around the critical point. The same behaviour of fQf_{\text{Q}} is observed at 𝒌=(π,0)\bm{k}=(\pi,0), which exhibits a vanishing exponent νQ=−0.02±0.06\nu_{\text{Q}}=-0.02\pm 0.06 around the critical point xc=0.08x_{\text{c}}=0.08.

To conclude, we find that the QFI density is capable to detect the quantum phase transitions at T=0T=0 in the random-plaquette model. Given an ordering wave vector 𝒌\bm{k}, the scaling exponent of fQf_{\text{Q}} with respect to the system size vanishes across the transition point xcx_{\text{c}}:

νQ​(𝒌)|x=xc≈0,\left.\nu_{\text{Q}}(\bm{k})\right|_{x=x_{\text{c}}}\approx 0, (22)

which signifies the other magnetically ordered phase. It is noted that the scaling exponent of fQf_{\text{Q}} also vanishes at topological phase transitions, e.g. in the Kitaev superconducting chain [32]. Through Eq. 22, we extend the universality of this phenomenon to the order-disorder phase transitions in 2D random quantum magnets.

IV Statistics of randomness-induced frustration

Extra insights can be gained on the role of the mixing ratio xx in Sr2CuTe1-xWxO6 by introducing the frustration index of a random instance. Illustrated in Fig. 9 (a), for each random instance of our model in Eq. 1, we consider a graph whose edges only contain the large couplings J1J_{1} and J2J_{2}, and omit the small ones J1′J^{\prime}_{1}, J2′J^{\prime}_{2}, and J1′′J^{\prime\prime}_{1}. The frustration index NFN_{\text{F}} is defined to be the minimal number of edges one needs to remove to make the graph geometrically non-frustrated (containing only even-length cycles of AFM couplings). In this simple example, we have NF=2N_{F}=2. In generic cases, the method to compute it is equivalent to finding the ground state of a classical AFM Ising model on the graph, and to solving other well-studied combinatorial optimization problems such as max-cut [76].

In the random-plaquette model, it is more convenient to consider the normalized frustration index nF=NF/Nn_{\text{F}}=N_{\text{F}}/N, which converges in the thermodynamic limit N→∞N\to\infty. Shown in Fig. 9 (b), when nFn_{\text{F}} is small (<0.1<0.1), the system exhibits the Néel or the stripe order. Each frustrated edge raises the ground state energy approximately by 2​J​|S|​(|S|+1)2J|S|(|S|+1), where J=J1J=J_{1} or J2J_{2} depending on the position of the frustrated edge, and |S|=1/2|S|=1/2. Remarkably, when xx enters the nonmagnetic region [0.08,0.55][0.08,0.55], a high plateau of nFn_{\text{F}} appears with a peak around x=0.3x=0.3, where it has so far been identified with most significant disordered SLL signatures. We can thus gain a phenomenological understanding on the origin of the nonmagnetic phase in Sr2CuTe1-xWxO6: The mixing ratio xx induces additional frustration, which plays a more important role in driving the system into a short-range disordered SLL phase than the originally present weak couplings J1′J^{\prime}_{1}, J2′J^{\prime}_{2}, and J1′′J^{\prime\prime}_{1}.

Moreover, in Fig. 9 (c) we show the distribution of nearest-neighbour spin correlations of the random-plaquette model at varying xx for a system with N=32N=32 spins. The lower and the upper bounds ⟨𝑺i⋅𝑺j⟩∈[−3/4,1/4]\expectationvalue*{\bm{S}_i \cdot\bm{S}_j}\in[-3/4,1/4] are given by pure spin singlet and triplet pairs. The two sharp peaks at ⟨𝑺i⋅𝑺j⟩=−0.340\expectationvalue*{\bm{S}_i \cdot\bm{S}_j}=-0.340 and 00 appear in the Néel and the stripe phases respectively. There is a smooth transfer of probability density between them as xx changes. Interestingly, in the nonmagnetic region x∈[0.08,0.55]x\in[0.08,0.55], the distribution spans much broader, and at x=0.3x=0.3 there appear two peaks of almost equal height. Compared with the random-bond J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} model [53], we do not observe any major peak of ⟨𝑺i⋅𝑺j⟩∈[−0.2,−0.1]\expectationvalue*{\bm{S}_i \cdot\bm{S}_j}\in[-0.2,-0.1] as in random-singlet states, and there is also no visible peak at ⟨𝑺i⋅𝑺j⟩>0\expectationvalue*{\bm{S}_i \cdot\bm{S}_j}>0 as in spin-glass states. This distinguishes our nonmagnetic state from these two candidates.

V Discussion

To summarize, in this work we perform extensive ED studies of the random-plaquette J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} model with experimentally relevant parameters for the material Sr2CuTe1-xWxO6. We resolve the phase boundaries of a nonmagnetic state x∈[0.08,0.55]x\in[0.08,0.55] by the finite-size scaling of various order parameters. The intermediate phase is absent of long-range Néel and stripe orders, valence-bond glass order, as well as glassy dynamics. Yet, it still exhibits short-range spin-spin correlations and a broad tail in SdynS_{\text{dyn}}, which are characteristic of disordered SLL states. Deep inside the nonmagnetic phase around x=0.3x=0.3, the randomness-induced frustration index reaches the maximum, bringing a series of non-trivial features including almost uniform SstaS_{\text{sta}} (or equivalently, fQf_{\text{Q}}) over the BZ. The broad peaks in SdynS_{\text{dyn}} are also stretched away from the two ordering wave vectors 𝒌=(π,π)\bm{k}=(\pi,\pi) and (π,0)(\pi,0), marking the difference from magnon-like excitations.

Although the bond frustration from the small couplings J1′,J2′,J1′′J^{\prime}_{1},J^{\prime}_{2},J^{\prime\prime}_{1} is not strong enough to support an all-to-all disordered random-singlet state as qEA>0q_{\text{EA}}>0, the frustration index in the model increases with structured randomness, thus favoring a disordered SLL state. Finally, from the analysis of the QFI, the nonmagnetic phase is multipatite entangled, and the vanishing universal scaling exponent of the QFI density with respect to NN across phase transitions shows the robustness of our phase boundaries in the thermodynamic limit.

In future, one may generalize the calculation of the QFI to thermal equilibrium mixed states for T>0T>0, using Eq. 17 and the Hams–de Raedt method [77]. A perfect scaling collapse at low temperatures [32] is expected from vanishing critical exponent at T=0T=0, and will extend the critical-TT regime of the phase diagram in Fig. 1 (b). It is also possible to study the QFI far from equilibrium in our model using small-size ED clusters, e.g. N=10N=10 spins [78].

Going beyond ED, one may also apply variational Monte Carlo (VMC) to explore 2D random quantum magnets. The recently developed neural quantum states [79, 80], especially the transformer architectures [81, 82], can be expressive variational ansatzes to capture the rich complexity of the physical system. There have been successful attempts at applying neural quantum states to approximate the QSL state in the regular J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} Heisenberg model on the square lattice [66, 83, 84, 85], despite the nature of Dirac spin liquid is still under debate [86]. Given the flexibility of neural networks, the access to larger system sizes is envisioned, which enables one to further resolve the dispersion of the dynamical spin structure factor and the spin excitation gaps, casting more light on the nature of the nonmagnetic state.

Appendix A Finite-size scaling on frustrated random magnets

A.1 Choice of finite-size lattices

We choose a series of lattices with N≤32N\leq 32 to obtain enough data points from ED and extrapolate to N→∞N\to\infty, while maintaining the desired symmetries. Here we formalize the construction of such lattices.

The infinite square lattice can be covered by repeating parallelogram unit cells, whose shape is determined by the parameters aa, bb, cc, dd, and the number of lattice sites in each unit cell is N=a​c+b​dN=ac+bd, as shown in Fig. S1 (a). We denote such a parallelogram unit cell with PBC by the parallelogram lattice.

We want the parallelogram lattices to be as close to square lattices as possible. The quantities δ1=|a2+b2−c2−d2|\delta_{1}=|a^{2}+b^{2}-c^{2}-d^{2}| and δ2=|a​d−b​c|\delta_{2}=|ad-bc| are invariant under translations and reflections, where δ1=0\delta_{1}=0 only if the four edges of the parallelogram have the same length, and δ2=0\delta_{2}=0 only if the four angles are right. We heuristically define the non-squareness δ=14​δ1+δ2\delta=\frac{1}{4}\delta_{1}+\delta_{2}.

Not all the lattices have the topology to form the Néel and the stripe orderings. We denote a lattice is Néel-compatible if it is bipartite, and stripe-compatible if it has exactly two components (connected subgraphs that are mutually disconnected) with the same size and each component is bipartite. In corollary, a parallelogram lattice is Néel-compatible only if a+ba+b and c+dc+d are both even, and it is stripe-compatible only if aa, bb, cc, dd are all even.

For each system size NN, we choose the lattice that is both Néel- and stripe-compatible, and has minimal δ\delta. The chosen lattices are listed in Table S1, and the non-trivial shapes are shown in Fig. S1.

A.2 Details of ED computation

The ED is implemented using the software package lattice-symmetries [87], which is one of the most performant among available software of the kind to our knowledge. We apply zero total magnetization (SU​(2)\text{SU}(2) symmetry) and spin inversion symmetry to reduce the Hilbert space, and we have verified that all random instances have ground states in the even parity sector under spin inversion. Note that no translational or reflection symmetry can be applied because of the random plaquettes.

A.3 Averaged observables over random instances

We use stratified sampling to generate random instances of the Hamiltonian with various numbers of J2J_{2}-dominated plaquettes, then reweight them according to the binomial distribution when computing the averaged observables given the probability xx. Therefore, we can reuse the observable values of the instances for all values of xx, without recomputing the ED and the expectations.

For each k=0,1,…,Nk=0,1,\ldots,N, we generate Mk=min⁡(Mk​max,(Nk))M_{k}=\min(M_{k\text{max}},\binom{N}{k}) instances randomly without replacement, each with exactly kk J2J_{2}-dominated plaquettes. Here Mk​maxM_{k\text{max}} is the maximal number of instances for each kk limited by the computation budget, and the actual number MkM_{k} is also limited by the number of combinations (Nk)\binom{N}{k}. We take Mk​max=100M_{k\text{max}}=100 when N≤20N\leq 20, Mk​max=30M_{k\text{max}}=30 when N=24,28N=24,28, and Mk​max=10M_{k\text{max}}=10 when N=32N=32.

When computing an averaged observable [O]J=[⟨O⟩]J[O]_{J}=[\!\expectationvalue*{O}]_{J}, we first take a uniform average over instances with the same kk, then average over the binomial distribution of kk:

[O]J​(N,x)=∑kB⁡(k,N,x)​O¯k​(N),\displaystyle[O]_{J}(N,x)=\sum_{k}B(k,N,x)\bar{O}_{k}(N), (S1)
B⁡(k,N,x)=(Nk)​xk​(1−x)N−k,\displaystyle B(k,N,x)=\binom{N}{k}x^{k}(1-x)^{N-k}, (S2)
O¯k​(N)=1Mk​∑iOi,\displaystyle\bar{O}_{k}(N)=\frac{1}{M_{k}}\sum_{i}O_{i}, (S3)

where ii runs over all MkM_{k} instances whose number of J2J_{2}-dominated plaquettes equals kk, and Oi=⟨O⟩iO_{i}=\expectationvalue*{O}_{i} is the observable value of this instance. As OiO_{i} is independent of xx, we can reuse it for all values of xx. For each xx, we compute [O]J​(N,x)[O]_{J}(N,x) with finite values of NN, then extrapolate to [O]J(N→∞,x)[O]_{J}(N\to\infty,x), as in Fig. 2.

The standard error of this weighted average is given by

Oerr2​(N,x)=1Meff​(N,x)​∑kB⁡(k,N,x)​Ok​err2​(N),\displaystyle O_{\text{err}}^{2}(N,x)=\frac{1}{M_{\text{eff}}(N,x)}\sum_{k}B(k,N,x)O_{k\text{err}}^{2}(N), (S4)
Meff​(N,x)=1∑kB​(k,N,x)2,\displaystyle M_{\text{eff}}(N,x)=\frac{1}{\sum_{k}B(k,N,x)^{2}}, (S5)
Ok​err2​(N)=(1−Mk(Nk))​1Mk2​∑i(Oi−O¯k)2,\displaystyle O_{k\text{err}}^{2}(N)=\left(1-\frac{M_{k}}{\binom{N}{k}}\right)\frac{1}{M_{k}^{2}}\sum_{i}(O_{i}-\bar{O}_{k})^{2}, (S6)

where MeffM_{\text{eff}} is the effective sample size over the binomial distribution, and Mk/(Nk)M_{k}/\binom{N}{k} is the finite population correction. The error bars OerrO_{\text{err}} are shown in Fig. 2 when N<∞N<\infty and 0<x<10<x<1.

A.4 Uncertainty of extrapolation

We use linear regression to extrapolate observables to N→∞N\to\infty, and propagate uncertainties of both the averages over random instances and the regression.

Consider a linear regression with PP data points 𝒙=(x1,…,xP)⊤\bm{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{P})^{\top}, 𝒚=(y1,…,yP)⊤\bm{y}=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{P})^{\top}. The standard errors in 𝒚\bm{y} are 𝒚err=(yerr​1,…,yerr​P)⊤\bm{y}_{\text{err}}=(y_{\text{err}1},\ldots,y_{\text{err}P})^{\top}, and there is no error in 𝒙\bm{x}. We have

𝒚=𝑿​𝜷+ϵ,\bm{y}=\bm{X}\bm{\beta}+\bm{\epsilon}, (S7)

where 𝑿=(𝟏,𝒙)\bm{X}=(\bm{1},\bm{x}) is a P×2P\times 2 matrix including the constant term, 𝜷=(β0,β1)⊤\bm{\beta}=(\beta_{0},\beta_{1})^{\top} contains the intercept and the slope, and ϵ\bm{\epsilon} is the errors of regression. Note that ϵ\bm{\epsilon} is heteroscedastic and we cannot assume that all components of ϵ\bm{\epsilon} are from distributions with the same variance, because the deviation of 𝒚\bm{y} from the linear relation is caused by the finite size effect, whose strength changes with the system size.

The parameters are estimated by least squares:

𝜷=𝑿¯​𝒚,𝑿¯=(𝑿⊤​𝑿)−1​𝑿⊤,\bm{\beta}=\bar{\bm{X}}\bm{y},\quad\bar{\bm{X}}=(\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^{\top}, (S8)

where 𝑿¯\bar{\bm{X}} is the pseudoinverse of 𝑿\bm{X}. The variance matrix of parameters from the errors in 𝒚\bm{y} is

Var(1)⁡𝜷=𝑿¯​(diag⁡𝒚err)2​𝑿¯⊤,\Var^{(1)}\bm{\beta}=\bar{\bm{X}}(\diag\bm{y}_{\text{err}})^{2}\bar{\bm{X}}^{\top}, (S9)

and another contribution from the errors of regression is

Var(2)⁡𝜷=PP−2​𝑿¯​(diag⁡ϵ)2​𝑿¯⊤,\displaystyle\Var^{(2)}\bm{\beta}=\frac{P}{P-2}\bar{\bm{X}}(\diag\bm{\epsilon})^{2}\bar{\bm{X}}^{\top}, (S10)
ϵ=𝒚−𝑿​𝜷.\displaystyle\bm{\epsilon}=\bm{y}-\bm{X}\bm{\beta}. (S11)

The total variance Var⁡𝜷=Var(1)⁡𝜷+Var(2)⁡𝜷\Var\bm{\beta}=\Var^{(1)}\bm{\beta}+\Var^{(2)}\bm{\beta}, and the standard error of the intercept β0​err\beta_{0\text{err}} is the square root of its first component. The error bars β0​err\beta_{0\text{err}} are shown in Fig. 2 when N→∞N\to\infty.

Appendix B QFI density from dynamical spin structure factor

Here, we briefly review the approach [32, 36, 37] of obtaining the QFI density fQf_{\text{Q}} through the dynamical spin structure in Eq. 17. It assumes thermal ensembles at the equilibrium and adapts the fluctuation-dissipation theorem for non-symmetrized Sdyn​(𝒌,ω,T)S_{\text{dyn}}(\bm{k},\omega,T) [88].

Let us take a generator O=NSz†𝒌=∑i=1NSizei​𝒌⋅𝒓iO=\sqrt{N}S^{z\dagger}_{\bm{k}}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}S_{i}^{z}e^{i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{r}_{i}}. Considering the definition of QFI density fQ=fQ/Nf_{\text{Q}}=f_{\text{Q}}/N and the form of QFI in Eq. 16, we have

fQ​(𝒌,T)=2​∑λ,λ′(pλ−pλ′)2pλ+pλ′​|⟨λ|Sz†𝒌|λ′⟩|2.f_{\text{Q}}(\bm{k},T)=2\sum_{\lambda,\lambda^{\prime}}\frac{(p_{\lambda}-p_{\lambda^{\prime}})^{2}}{p_{\lambda}+p_{\lambda^{\prime}}}\left|\!\matrixelement{\lambda}{S^{z \dagger}_{\bm{k}}}{\lambda'}\right|^{2}. (S12)

It is convenient to introduce the dynamical susceptibility

χ(𝒌,ω,T)=i∫0∞Tr[ρ[S𝒌z†(t),S𝒌z(0)]]ei​ω​tdt,\chi(\bm{k},\omega,T)=i\int_{0}^{\infty}\Tr\left[\rho[S^{z\dagger}_{\bm{k}}(t),S^{z}_{\bm{k}}(0)]\right]e^{i\omega t}\differential t, (S13)

which, after taking the integral, shares the form

χ(𝒌,ω,T)=iπ∑λ,λ′\displaystyle\chi(\bm{k},\omega,T)=i\pi\sum_{\lambda,\lambda^{\prime}} (pλ−pλ′)​|⟨λ|Sz†𝒌(0)|λ′⟩|2\displaystyle(p_{\lambda}-p_{\lambda^{\prime}})\left|\!\matrixelement{\lambda}{S^{z \dagger}_{\bm{k}}(0)}{\lambda'}\right|^{2}
×δ⁡(ω+Eλ−Eλ′).\displaystyle\times\delta(\omega+E_{\lambda}-E_{\lambda^{\prime}}). (S14)

In reaching the form above, we have adopted the density matrix ρ=∑λpλ​|λ⟩​⟨λ|\rho=\sum_{\lambda}p_{\lambda}\ket{\lambda}\bra{\lambda} with pλ=1Ze−Eλ/Tp_{\lambda}=\frac{1}{Z}e^{-E_{\lambda}/T}, and inserted the identity 𝟙=∑λ′|λ′⟩​⟨λ′|\mathds{1}=\sum_{\lambda^{\prime}}\ket{\lambda'}\bra{\lambda'}. Comparing Eq. S14 with Eq. S12 and taking into account

pλ−pλ′pλ+pλ′=tanh⁡(Eλ′−Eλ2​T),\frac{p_{\lambda}-p_{\lambda^{\prime}}}{p_{\lambda}+p_{\lambda^{\prime}}}=\tanh(\frac{E_{\lambda'} - E_\lambda}{2 T}), (S15)

we arrive at

fQ​(𝒌,T)=4π​∫0∞tanh⁡(ω2​T)​χ′′​(ω,𝒌,T)​dω,f_{\text{Q}}(\bm{k},T)=\frac{4}{\pi}\int_{0}^{\infty}\tanh(\frac{\omega}{2 T})\chi^{\prime\prime}(\omega,\bm{k},T)\,\differential\omega, (S16)

where χ′′\chi^{\prime\prime} denotes the imaginary (dissipative) part of the dynamical susceptibility.

On the other hand, one can also relate χ′′\chi^{\prime\prime} to the non-symmetrized dynamical spin structure in Eq. 14 through the fluctuation-dissipation theorem. Starting from the integral definition of χ\chi in Eq. S13, it is straightforward to identify that

χ′′​(𝒌,ω,T)=12​(g1​(𝒌,ω,T)−g2​(𝒌,ω,T)),\chi^{\prime\prime}(\bm{k},\omega,T)=\frac{1}{2}\left(g_{1}(\bm{k},\omega,T)-g_{2}(\bm{k},\omega,T)\right), (S17)

with

g1​(𝒌,ω,T)\displaystyle g_{1}(\bm{k},\omega,T) =∫−∞∞⟨Sz†𝒌(t)Sz𝒌(0)⟩​ei​ω​t​dt,\displaystyle=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\!\expectationvalue*{S^{z \dagger}_{\bm{k}}(t) S^z_{\bm{k}}(0)}e^{i\omega t}\,\differential t,
g2​(𝒌,ω,T)\displaystyle g_{2}(\bm{k},\omega,T) =∫−∞∞⟨Sz𝒌(0)Sz†𝒌(t)⟩​ei​ω​t​dt.\displaystyle=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\!\expectationvalue*{S^z_{\bm{k}}(0) S^{z \dagger}_{\bm{k}}(t)}e^{i\omega t}\,\differential t. (S18)

The notation ⟨⋯⟩=Tr[ρ⋯]\expectationvalue*{\cdots}=\Tr[\rho\cdots] is adopted for a thermal state. Since g1=2​π​Sdyng_{1}=2\pi S_{\text{dyn}}, if we can further associate g2g_{2} with g1g_{1}, our goal will be accomplished. It is again more convenient to compare these two quantities after integration. It turns out that

g2​(𝒌,ω,T)\displaystyle g_{2}(\bm{k},\omega,T) =∑λ,λ′e−Eλ′/TZ​|⟨λ|Sz†𝒌(0)|λ′⟩|2\displaystyle=\sum_{\lambda,\lambda^{\prime}}\frac{e^{-E_{\lambda^{\prime}}/T}}{Z}\left|\!\matrixelement{\lambda}{S^{z \dagger}_{\bm{k}}(0)}{\lambda'}\right|^{2}
×2​π​δ​(ω+Eλ−Eλ′)\displaystyle\phantom{{}=\sum_{\lambda,\lambda^{\prime}}}\times 2\pi\delta(\omega+E_{\lambda}-E_{\lambda^{\prime}})
=e−ωT​g1​(𝒌,ω,T).\displaystyle=e^{-\frac{\omega}{T}}g_{1}(\bm{k},\omega,T). (S19)

Thus we obtain the adapted fluctuation-dissipation theorem,

χ′′​(𝒌,ω,T)=π⁡(1−e−ωT)​Sdyn​(𝒌,ω,T).\chi^{\prime\prime}(\bm{k},\omega,T)=\pi\left(1-e^{-\frac{\omega}{T}}\right)S_{\text{dyn}}(\bm{k},\omega,T). (S20)

Combining Eqs. S16 and S20, the entanglement witness fQf_{\text{Q}} is reconstructed from the quantum fluctuations contained in SdynS_{\text{dyn}}, and we reach Eq. 17:

fQ​(𝒌,T)=4​∫0∞tanh⁡(ω2​T)⁡(1−e−ωT)​Sdyn​(𝒌,ω,T)​dω.f_{\text{Q}}(\bm{k},T)=4\int_{0}^{\infty}\!\!\tanh(\frac{\omega}{2 T})\left(1-e^{-\frac{\omega}{T}}\right)S_{\text{dyn}}(\bm{k},\omega,T)\,\differential\omega. (S21)
